name: Ananya Iyer
headline: VP Sales, institutional healthcare consumables
samplePosts:
Our western region team closed a difficult renewal this quarter, and very little of it was about price.

The hospital's infection-control nurse had been raising the same two issues for months. Nobody senior had sat with her. Our area manager did, twice, and came back with a change to how we train ward staff, not a discount.

The renewal followed. So did a referral to a sister hospital.

I keep relearning that in institutional sales the person with the problem is rarely the person who signs. Finding them is the job.

Who in your buying chain do you speak to least?

We stopped celebrating order value in our weekly review and started looking at how many accounts had a second contact we trusted.

It felt slower for a month. Then forecast accuracy improved, because a single relationship leaving no longer meant a lost account.

Credit to our regional heads, who pushed back on the change and then made it work better than I had designed it.

If you lead a field team, what do you review every week that you suspect does not matter?
styleNotes: Ends with a question to other sales leaders

name: Rahul Menon
headline: Director of Engineering, B2B SaaS platform
samplePosts:
We cut our on-call pages by 41% in two quarters without hiring anyone.

The change was boring: every alert needed an owner and a written action. If nobody could say what to do when it fired, we deleted it.

We deleted 63 alerts in the first month. Two came back. The rest were noise we had learned to tolerate.

The bigger effect was on people. Engineers stopped dreading their on-call week, and two of them now run the alert review themselves.

What is one alert your team has learned to ignore?

I used to think senior engineers grew by owning bigger systems. Now I think they grow by owning clearer decisions.

This quarter I asked each senior engineer to write one decision record a month: the options, what we chose, and what would make us change our mind.

The documents were short. The discussions they started were not. Three of them changed our roadmap.

If you manage engineers, how do you make their judgement visible?
styleNotes: Uses 'I' for his own decisions, 'we' for the team

name: Meera Kapoor
headline: Financial Controller, auto components
pillars: Finance teams that partner with operations
samplePosts:
Our month-end close now takes about half the time it did last year. Most of the gain came from a conversation, not a system.

The plant accountants and the central team had been reconciling the same inventory numbers separately, then arguing about the differences. We agreed one owner per account and one cut-off time.

The arguments stopped. The close got shorter. The team got its evenings back.

The lesson for me: before automating a process, check whether two groups are quietly doing the same work.

A junior analyst on my team found an error in a supplier rebate calculation that had gone unnoticed for several quarters.

She did not just flag it. She traced how it happened, proposed a control, and walked the procurement team through it.

That is the kind of ownership I hope to see more of, and it rarely shows up in a job description.

How do you recognise this kind of work in your teams?
styleNotes: Uses relative numbers, never exact figures

name: James Whitfield
headline: Head of Digital Transformation, retail banking
samplePosts:
The most useful thing we did on our last programme was cancel a feature everyone wanted.

It had a sponsor, a budget and a launch date. It also depended on a core system that could not change safely before the end of the year. We said so early, in writing, and moved the money to fixing the complaints journey instead.

Complaints resolved at first contact went up by about a third. Nobody remembers the feature.

Transformation is mostly choosing what not to do. What have you stopped recently?

I spent a morning in one of our contact centres last week, wearing a headset and listening.

Three calls in a row were about the same letter. It was accurate, compliant and completely unclear. The team had raised it months ago.

We rewrote it with them that afternoon. The lesson was not about letters; it was about how far away the people who can fix things sit from the people who hear the problem.

When did you last listen to your own customers' calls?
styleNotes: Never makes claims about products or rates

name: Fiona Clarke
headline: Programme Director, digital health
samplePosts:
I'll be honest: our first version of the new discharge checklist was a failure.

We designed it in meeting rooms. On the wards it took nurses longer than the paper form it replaced, so they quietly went back to paper.

Version two was designed on a night shift, with the people who use it. It takes four minutes instead of eleven, and 92% of discharges now use it.

I'm proud of the team, and a bit embarrassed it took us a failure to go and ask. What did your last failure teach you?

Today a ward sister told me our new rota tool gave her back an hour a week.

That hour is why we do this. Not the dashboards, not the launch event. An hour that goes back to patients and to the people caring for them.

Huge thanks to the clinical informatics team, who sat through every complaint and kept going.

If you work in health tech: how do you measure the time you give back?

name: Daniel Ortiz
headline: Director, Wealth Management
samplePosts:
The hardest planning conversations I have are rarely about money. They are about who decides when the founder steps back.

This year I started asking families to write down, separately, what they think the plan is. The answers almost never match. That gap is where the real work starts.

None of this shows up in a performance report, but it is often the most valuable hour we spend together.

What question has changed the way you advise families?

One of the advisors I mentor led her first family meeting on her own this month.

She did something I did not teach her: she paused the agenda to ask the adult children what worried them. The meeting ran long and the family left with fewer questions than they arrived with.

Mentoring works best when the person you mentor ends up teaching you something.

Who taught you the most early in your career?
styleNotes: Never mentions performance, returns or products

name: Sarah Kim
headline: Principal, operations strategy consulting
samplePosts:
The best recommendation our team made this year was smaller than the one the client asked for.

They wanted a network redesign. The data said two distribution centers were fine; the problem was how orders were batched. We recommended changing the batching rules first and revisiting the network in a year.

It saved most of the cost the redesign would have, in about a tenth of the time.

I think the most valuable thing a consultant can say is sometimes 'not yet.' When has a smaller answer been the right one for you?

A first-year analyst on my team rebuilt our model so a plant manager could run it himself.

It was less elegant. It was also the only version that got used after we left.

I now ask every team the same question before a final presentation: who will open this file after we're gone, and can they?

What do you do to make sure your work outlives the project?
styleNotes: Credits junior team members by role

name: Marcus Bell
headline: VP Product, healthtech
samplePosts:
We killed a feature this week that took us three months to build. And honestly? It was the right call.

Usage looked great in the demo. In real clinics, nurses used it once and never again, because it added two clicks to a task they do forty times a shift.

We should have watched a full shift before building anything. Now we do, for every feature.

Shout-out to our design team, who argued for this from day one. What's a feature you were glad to kill?

Our product team now spends one day a month in a clinic. No laptops, just notebooks.

The first visit was humbling. Half of our roadmap assumptions didn't survive lunch.

The second visit gave us our best quarter of discovery yet: three problems nobody had put in a ticket.

If you build for clinicians, how often do you watch them work?

name: Layla Haddad
headline: Fractional CMO for growth-stage consumer brands
samplePosts:
A founder asked me last month why their ads stopped working. The ads were fine. The promise had drifted.

Over two years the brand had added four new customer segments, and the message tried to speak to all of them. It ended up speaking to none.

We went back to the first hundred customers, interviewed twenty of them, and rebuilt the message around the one thing they all mentioned. Cost per lead fell by about a third within two months.

When did you last ask your earliest customers why they chose you?

Most marketing teams I join have a strategy problem that looks like a resourcing problem.

They ask for more people. What they need first is fewer priorities.

In my first month with any client, I try to cut the plan to three things the whole team can name without looking. It is uncomfortable, and it works more often than hiring does.

What would your team say your top three priorities are?
styleNotes: Starts with a client situation, anonymised

name: Omar Saeed
headline: Project Director, major infrastructure
samplePosts:
On large projects, the schedule rarely slips in one big event. It slips in a hundred small decisions nobody wants to escalate.

This year our site teams started a ten-minute daily review of decisions waiting more than two days. Most were resolved in the room.

We recovered several weeks of float over the quarter, and the teams say the site feels calmer.

I am grateful to the site engineers who made this a habit rather than another meeting.

Our best safety improvement this year came from a junior supervisor, not a policy.

He noticed that near-miss reports dropped whenever a senior visitor was on site, because people did not want to look careless. He suggested anonymous reporting cards at every gate.

Reports went up sharply. Incidents went down.

The people closest to the work usually see the problem first. Our job is to make it safe for them to say so.
styleNotes: British spelling, no questions at the end

name: Wei Ling Tan
headline: Regional HR Director, APAC
samplePosts:
We rewrote our performance review form from twelve questions to three. Managers were sceptical. Then the conversations got better.

The three questions: what went well, what got in the way, and what you need from me next quarter. Everything else was moved to an optional appendix nobody misses.

Completion went up, and the comments got longer and more specific.

My takeaway: the form shapes the conversation more than the training does. What question would you add?

Our warehouse supervisors in five countries now meet once a month, without HR in the room.

We set it up, then stepped out. They swap rota ideas, safety fixes and the occasional complaint about head office.

Two of their ideas are now standard practice across the region, and attrition among new supervisors has come down noticeably.

Sometimes the most useful thing HR can do is create the room and leave it.
styleNotes: Lists in plain sentences, no bullets

name: Arjun Nair
headline: Head of Compliance, payments
samplePosts:
Our compliance team now sits in product planning from the first sketch, not the final review.

It felt slow at first. Then launch delays from late compliance findings dropped to almost none, because the questions were answered while they were still cheap to change.

The product managers asked for it to continue, which I count as the real measure.

Compliance that arrives early is advice. Compliance that arrives late is a veto.

I asked my team to rewrite our onboarding policy so a new joiner could follow it without asking anyone.

The new version is a third of the length, and the number of questions new joiners raise in their first month has fallen.

Credit to the analyst who led it and tested every step with someone from the customer support team.

Clear policies are a form of respect for the people who have to follow them.
